ruling.explanation: The rule in ## making-an-attack > melee-attacks > grappling explicitly states that 'When you move, you can drag or carry the grappled creature with you'. The fact from the question is that the user is grappling a creature and wants to know if they can drag it while moving. The conclusion is yes, because the rule allows dragging a grappled creature during movement.

The rule for escaping a grapple states that the target must succeed on a Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics) check contested by the grappler's Strength (Athletics) check. The text explicitly lists both ability options, allowing the creature to choose which one to use.

The rule for grappling states that 'The target of your grapple must be no more than one size larger than you'. The question asks about grappling a creature 'two sizes larger' than the grappler. Since 'two sizes larger' exceeds the limit of 'no more than one size larger', the action is not allowed.

The rule 'making-an-attack > melee-attacks > grappling' states that making a grapple requires 'Using at least one free hand'. The question asks if you can hold a grapple (implying the condition is active) and attack with a two-handed weapon. To attack with a two-handed weapon, you must wield it with two hands ('weapon-properties > two-handed'). If you are grappling, you are using at least one hand to seize the target. Therefore, you cannot use that same hand for the two-handed weapon, nor can you use both hands of the grappled creature (as they are not yours). The text allows no other reading where a single free hand is sufficient to wield a two-handed weapon while maintaining a grapple.

The question asks if a creature that is both grappled and prone can stand up after being shoved. The rule 'making-an-attack > melee-attacks > shoving-a-creature' states that if you win the shove contest, you can push the target 5 feet away from you. The rule 'conditions > grappled' states that the condition ends if an effect removes the grappled creature from the reach of the grappler or grappling effect, such as when a creature is hurled away. Pushing a creature 5 feet away (if it was within reach) removes it from the reach of the grappler, ending the grapple. The rule 'movement-and-position > being-prone' states that standing up costs movement equal to half your speed and you can't stand up if your speed is 0. However, the rule 'conditions > grappled' also says a grappled creature's speed becomes 0. If the grapple ends due to the shove, the creature is no longer grappled, so its speed is no longer 0 (unless another effect reduced it). Therefore, once the grapple ends via the shove, the creature can attempt to stand up if it has enough movement left. The question asks 'Can it stand up?', implying possibility. Since the shove ends the grapple, and standing up is possible if movement remains, the answer is yes.

The question asks 'What is rolled?', which is a what question. The rule in 'making-an-attack > making-an-attack' states that if you're making an attack roll, you're making an attack. The rule in 'casting-a-spell > spell-attack-rolls' states that some spells require the caster to make an attack roll. The rule in 'damage-and-healing > damage-rolls' states that you roll the damage die or dice. Since the question asks what is rolled during an attack, the answer is an attack roll and potentially a damage roll.

The rule 'using-each-ability > dexterity > hiding' states that you can't hide from a creature that can see you clearly, but it does not forbid hiding in a lightly obscured area. The rule 'the-environment > vision-and-light' defines a lightly obscured area (like dim light) as one where creatures have disadvantage on Perception checks, implying vision is not blocked entirely. Therefore, since the area is not heavily obscured (which blocks vision entirely), you can attempt to hide there.

The question asks what is rolled for an attack roll under specific conditions (ranged, 5 feet, target prone). The rule 'making-an-attack > attack-rolls' states that to make an attack roll, you roll a d20 and add modifiers. The rules regarding disadvantage ('making-an-attack > ranged-attacks > ranged-attacks-in-close-combat', 'conditions > prone') and advantage ('conditions > prone') modify the outcome of the roll (adding or subtracting modifiers) but do not change the fundamental action of rolling a d20. The rule 'spells > true-strike' mentions gaining advantage, which also modifies the roll's success chance but not the die itself. Therefore, regardless of the modifiers applied by being prone or close range, the physical object rolled is a d20.

The rule for death saving throws states that rolling a 1 counts as two failures, while rolling a 20 regains hit points. The general rule for saving throws says to roll a d20 and add modifiers, but does not specify the outcome of natural 1s or 20s for all saves. The text allows another reading where only death saving throws have special rules for natural 1s and 20s, while other saving throws follow standard success/failure based on DC. Since the text does not explicitly state that a natural 1 always fails for all saving throws, there is ambiguity.

The rule 'casting-a-spell > duration > concentration' states that 'Being incapacitated or killed. You lose concentration on a spell if you are incapacitated or if you die.' The fact from the question is that the creature was knocked unconscious, which implies being incapacitated. Therefore, being knocked unconscious ends concentration.

The rule states that if you cast a spell with a bonus action, you cannot cast another spell during the same turn except for a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action. The fact is that the user cast a spell as a bonus action and wants to know if they can cast a cantrip with their action. The conclusion is yes, because the rule explicitly allows casting a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action after casting a bonus action spell.

The question asks if releasing a readied spell counts against the rule that limits casting spells with a bonus action. The 'actions-in-combat > ready' entry states that when you ready a spell, you cast it as normal but hold its energy, releasing it with your reaction. The 'casting-a-spell > casting-time > bonus-action' entry rules that if you cast a spell with a bonus action, you can't cast another spell during the same turn except for a cantrip with a casting time of 1 action. Since releasing a readied spell uses a reaction (not a bonus action), it does not trigger the restriction on casting another spell with a bonus action or vice versa in the same turn context described by the bonus-action rule. The 'actions-in-combat > cast-a-spell' entry confirms that casting a spell is not necessarily an action and depends on the casting time. Therefore, releasing a readied spell (a reaction) does not count against the bonus-action spell rule because they are different types of actions/reactions.

The rule for making an opportunity attack states that you can make one when a hostile creature 'that you can see' moves out of your reach. The question asks about attacking a creature 'I can't see'. Since the rule explicitly requires the creature to be visible, it does not apply to an unseen creature. Therefore, you cannot make an opportunity attack against a creature you can't see based on this text.

The rule states that you can move through a nonhostile creature's space, but only if the creature is at least two sizes larger or smaller than you for hostile creatures. It also says you can't willingly end your move in any creature's space. The Disengage action prevents opportunity attacks when moving out of reach, but it does not change the rules about moving through a creature's space. Therefore, even after Disengaging, you cannot move through an enemy's space unless they are at least two sizes larger or smaller than you.

The rule 'movement-and-position > moving-around-other-creatures' states that 'another creature's space is difficult terrain for you.' The fact from the question is that the ally is a creature. Therefore, moving through an ally's space counts as difficult terrain.

The rule 'movement-and-position > breaking-up-your-move > moving-between-attacks' explicitly states that if you take an action including more than one weapon attack, you can break up your movement by moving between those attacks. The fact from the question is asking about the possibility of moving between attacks. Therefore, the conclusion is yes.

The rule states that 'A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.' The fact from the question is that one member spots the ambush (is not surprised) while others are in an ambush situation. The conclusion is that the whole party is not necessarily surprised because one member spotting it means at least some members are not surprised, and the rule explicitly allows for mixed states of surprise within a group.

The rule 'movement-and-position > flying-movement' states that if a flying creature is knocked prone, it falls unless it has the ability to hover or is being held aloft by magic. The question asks what happens when a flying creature is knocked prone. The text allows another reading where the creature might have the ability to hover or be held aloft by magic, which would prevent falling. However, the question does not specify these conditions, so we assume they are not present. Therefore, the creature falls.

The rule states that 'Whenever you take damage while you are concentrating on a spell, you must make a Constitution saving throw to maintain your concentration.' It also specifies that if damage comes from multiple sources, 'you make a separate saving throw for each source of damage.' The fact is that the user was hit by three separate bolts at once. Therefore, the conclusion is that three saves are required.

The rule for opportunity attacks states that when a hostile creature moves out of your reach, you use your reaction to make one melee attack against it. The rule for grappling states that you can use the Attack action to make a special melee attack called a grapple. Since an opportunity attack is defined as making a 'melee attack' and not specifically the 'Attack action', and the grapple requires using the 'Attack action', the text does not allow replacing the opportunity attack with a grapple.

The rule for Ready states that when you ready an action, you choose 'the action you will take in response to that trigger.' The rule for the Attack action states it makes one or more attacks depending on features like Extra Attack. However, the rule for Ready does not specify that you can ready a specific multi-attack version of an action (like 'Attack with Extra Attack') and then execute all those attacks upon the trigger; rather, you choose the action type to be taken later. While the text allows choosing the action, it implies the action is resolved as defined by its current state or standard definition at the time of resolution. The critical ambiguity lies in whether 'choose the action' includes choosing a specific instance of that action with all its potential modifiers (like Extra Attack) locked in, or if you simply choose the base action type and resolve it normally. Given the phrasing 'choose the action you will take', one reading is you choose the base 'Attack' action, which resolves to 1 attack unless modified by features active at that moment. Another reading is you choose the full capability of the action. However, standard interpretation of 'Ready' usually implies readying a single reaction event. The text for Ready says 'choose the action you will take'. The text for Attack says 'With this action, you make one melee or ranged attack.' It also says 'Certain features... allow you to make more than one attack'. If you ready the 'Attack' action, do you ready the ability to make multiple attacks? The text does not explicitly say you can't. But it also doesn't say you can. This creates ambiguity on whether the 'Extra Attack' feature applies to a readied action. Since the text allows reading that you choose the base action (which is 1 attack) and another reading that you choose the full capability, and the text does not decide between them explicitly regarding readied multi-attacks, this is ambiguous.

The rule 'casting-a-spell > targets > targeting-yourself' states that if a spell targets a creature of your choice, you can choose yourself unless the creature must be hostile or specifically a creature other than you. It also says if you are in the area of effect of a spell you cast, you can target yourself. The rule 'spells > fireball' describes an explosion centered on a point you choose, affecting creatures in that area. The question asks if you can choose to leave yourself out of your own fireball. Since fireball targets a point and affects creatures in the area, not specifically targeting a creature (like 'magic missile'), the rule about choosing yourself applies to spells that target a creature. However, for area-of-effect spells like fireball, the text does not explicitly say you can exclude yourself from the area of effect once cast. The rule 'casting-a-spell > targets > targeting-yourself' allows you to target yourself if the spell targets a creature of your choice, but fireball targets a point in space, not a creature directly. Therefore, the question is ambiguous because the text does not explicitly address whether you can exclude yourself from an area-of-effect spell like fireball once cast.

The rule states that when you take a reaction, you can't take another one until the start of your next turn. The fact is that the user used their reaction in round 1 and an enemy acts before them in round 2. The conclusion is that they cannot make an opportunity attack because they have no reactions left until the start of their next turn.

The rule 'spells > shield' states that when you cast Shield, 'you have a +5 bonus to AC, including against the triggering attack'. The fact from the question is that an attack hits you and you subsequently cast Shield. The conclusion is that the +5 AC applies because the rule explicitly includes the triggering attack in the bonus.

The rule states that if a creature is casting a spell of 3rd level or lower, Counterspell interrupts it automatically. The fact from the question is that the enemy is casting Cure Wounds using a 5th-level slot. According to the rule 'Casting a Spell at a Higher Level', when a spellcaster casts a spell using a slot of a higher level than the spell, the spell assumes the higher level for that casting. Therefore, the Cure Wounds spell being cast with a 5th-level slot is considered a 5th-level spell. Since 5th level is greater than 3rd level, Counterspell does not stop it automatically; an ability check would be required if the caster's spellcasting ability meets the DC.

The rule 'class-features > warlock > eldritch-invocation-eldritch-sight' states that a Warlock can cast detect magic at will, without expending a spell slot. The fact from the question is that the user wants to know if Detect Magic can be cast without spending a spell slot. The conclusion is yes for a Warlock with this feature. However, the rule 'what-is-a-spell > rituals' states that ritual spells don't expend a spell slot but require a feature to grant the ability to do so, and 'detect-magic' has the ritual tag. The fact from the question does not specify if the user is casting it as a ritual or using a Warlock feature. Since the text allows for both readings (casting without a slot via ritual or via Warlock feature), and the text does not decide between them for a general 'can I' question without specifying class or method, this is ambiguous.

The rule under ## spells > invisibility states that 'The spell ends for a target that attacks or casts a spell.' Therefore, if you are currently under the effect of the Invisibility spell and you make an attack, the spell ends immediately before or as the attack is made. Since the spell ends, you are no longer invisible at the moment the attack resolves. Consequently, you do not have advantage on the attack roll because the condition for having advantage (being unseen by the target) is lost when you attack.

The rule states that for *fireball*, the target is a point in space where the ball of fire erupts, and the spell description says the fire spreads around corners. The fact from the question is that the creature is around a corner with no straight line to it. The conclusion is that the creature is caught because the spell's effect (the explosion) spreads around corners, meaning the lack of a straight line does not prevent the target from being affected.

The rule for 'equipment > net' states that when you use an action to attack with a net, 'you can make only one attack regardless of the number of attacks you can normally make.' The fact from the question is that the user can attack twice (via Extra Attack). The conclusion is that even though multiple attacks are allowed by class features, the specific rule for nets limits the usage to a single attack per turn. Therefore, throwing two nets is not allowed.

The rule states that a Large or smaller creature hit by a net is restrained until freed. The fact from the question is that the user hit a Large creature with a net. Therefore, the creature suffers being restrained. To get free, the creature can use its action to make a DC 10 Strength check, or deal 5 slashing damage to the net (AC 10).

answer.verdict: The Large creature is restrained. It gets free by making a DC 10 Strength check or taking 5 slashing damage to the net.

ruling.explanation: The rule 'making-an-attack > ranged-attacks > ranged-attacks-in-close-combat' states that you have disadvantage on a ranged attack if you are within 5 feet of a hostile creature who can see you. The fact from the question is that the enemy is standing right next to you (within 5 feet). Therefore, the conclusion is yes, you have disadvantage.

The rule 'making-an-attack > melee-attacks' states that an unarmed strike is a punch, kick, head-butt, or similar forceful blow and explicitly notes '(none of which count as weapons)'. The question asks if a handaxe (which is a weapon) can be thrown as a bonus attack. While the 'making-an-attack > melee-attacks' rule defines unarmed strikes, it does not prohibit throwing a held weapon that has the 'thrown' property. The 'weapon-properties > thrown' rule states 'If a weapon has the thrown property, you can throw the weapon to make a ranged attack.' The 'equipment > handaxe' entry confirms a handaxe has the 'Thrown' property. Therefore, the text allows throwing the handaxe. There is no conflict regarding whether a weapon with the thrown property can be thrown; the only potential ambiguity in the provided text is the definition of unarmed strikes versus weapons, but since a handaxe is explicitly a weapon and not an unarmed strike, the rule about unarmed strikes does not apply to prevent the throw. The text allows another reading (that you cannot throw anything) only if one misinterprets 'melee attacks' as excluding ranged throws of weapons, but the 'thrown' property rule clarifies this.

The rule for Sneak Attack states that you can deal extra damage if you have advantage on the attack roll OR if another enemy is within 5 feet of the target (and other conditions are met). The question specifies the rogue has advantage and attacks with a longsword. However, the Rogue class feature requires the attack to use a 'finesse or a ranged weapon'. A longsword does not have the finesse property (unlike a rapier or dagger), nor is it a ranged weapon. Therefore, even with advantage, the specific requirement for the weapon type is not met. The rule on Advantage and Disadvantage confirms that having advantage allows rolling two d20s and using the higher one, but does not override the weapon property requirement for Sneak Attack.

The rule for Sneak Attack states you gain advantage if another enemy of the target is within 5 feet of it and isn't incapacitated, regardless of your own position or disadvantage. The fact from the question is that an orc (an enemy) is standing next to the goblin (the target). This satisfies the condition for extra damage even though the user has disadvantage due to being close to the ally.

The rule states that Martial Arts applies when wielding 'monk weapons', which are defined as shortswords and any simple melee weapons that don't have the two-handed or heavy property. A greatclub is a simple melee weapon but has the Two-Handed property. Therefore, it does not meet the criteria for a monk weapon, and the Martial Arts feature cannot be used with it.

The rule for the Great Weapon Fighting fighting style states that you can reroll a damage die when rolling a 1 or 2 on an attack made with a melee weapon wielded with two hands, provided the weapon has the two-handed or versatile property. The fact from the question is that the character is a fighter wielding a longsword in both hands. A longsword has the versatile property and deals 1d8 slashing damage (or 1d10 when used two-handed), meaning it qualifies for the Great Weapon Fighting benefit when held with two hands. Therefore, the conclusion is yes.

The user asks about the spell slots of a paladin 4/sorcerer 3. The rule 'multiclassing > class-features > spellcasting > spell-slots' states that for multiclassing, you add levels in bard, cleric, druid, sorcerer, and wizard classes, plus half (rounded down) of levels in paladin and ranger classes to determine the total character level for the Multiclass Spellcaster table. The user is a paladin 4 and sorcerer 3, totaling 7 levels.
